To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the ASCUS- LSIL Triage Study data can be used to adjust for lead time bias and other potential sources of error and/or bias in a simplified economic analysis of age-based management of LSIL, and that 2) the results of the economic analysis change following adjustment, with the rank ordering of the 3 management strategies changing in the 2 younger age groups.

(a) the rank order of age-based management options for women with LSIL changes after adjustment for potential bias in the ASCUS- LSIL Triage Study and (b) the adjusted results are consistent with the results of the study’s cost-effectiveness analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of how to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of health care interventions in situations in which there are no randomized trials.
how the results of randomized clinical trials may be adjusted for potential bias and random error in order to inform policy makers.
the problem of adjusting data from RCTs for use in economic evaluation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cost-effectiveness of a management strategy is not known, and further research is required to determine the optimal management strategy.
the results of this study are consistent with those of other studies, but the data are not conclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found the adjusted data to be more realistic and more consistent with our understanding of the underlying processes.
the ASCUS- LSIL Triage Study was well-designed and conducted.
the decision to adjust trial data for economic evaluation depends on the nature of the intervention and the trial design.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decision analyst must be vigilant about potential sources of bias in trial data and must be able to identify and adjust for them in order to produce accurate results for policy analysis.
decision analysts should consider adjusting trial data when the study design and/or results suggest that random error or bias may exist.
decision analysts need to examine trial design and data carefully to detect evidence of bias and adjust for bias when appropriate.
